title: Stolin Hasidism and the many strands of religious life in David-Horodok
summary: The memorial book portrays Hasidism as a distinctive part of local Jewish religious life and ties the town to the neighboring Stolin center.

editorialConnections.recordTitle: Hasidim pass through the town toward Stolin

editorialContent:
## A small town, several religious centers

Religious life in [David-Horodok](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_1ffa438353dc176e94f25c7d) was not represented by one congregation or a single rabbinic voice. The memorial book, in JewishGen’s translation, recalls several synagogues and study houses: the Great Synagogue, the Great Beth Midrash, the rabbi’s study house, a synagogue of Stolin Hasidim, and a synagogue of the town’s wealthy donors. It also describes a separate prayer room in the home of Reb Itzikl, where his Hasidim gathered. These institutions made religious affiliation visible in daily town life, while leaving room for shared worship, study, and civic ties.

The book calls the Stolin Hasidim a sizable part of the town’s population, yet another passage characterizes the Hasidic presence as relatively small and weakly influential. Those descriptions need not cancel each other out: “sizable” may refer to one faction among local Jews, while limited influence describes Hasidism’s place in the town as a whole. The evidence does not provide a reliable percentage. Nor should the [Stolin Hasidim](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_805a7fb10f0335f9a38f4861) be confused with the town’s distinct Horodoker Hasidic dynasty, whose rebbe and followers were rooted in David-Horodok itself.

The memorial book names people who gave these buildings their particular sound. At the Stolin Hasidim’s synagogue, prayer leaders included Avraham Moshe the teacher, Yosef Chasha-Bashe’s (Shatzki), Izel, Moshe and Yosef Kolozny, Yudel Shatzki, Asher Margolin, Yaakov Begun, Yaakov Milman the blacksmith, and Mordechai Begun. Elsewhere, Yehudovitz’s initiative and donations supported the Great Study House, also known as Yehudovitz’s Study House. The community’s religious landscape was therefore built not only by rabbis, but by donors, teachers, tradespeople, cantors, and congregants.

## Stolin nearby, and a local Hasidic dynasty

Stolin’s importance rested partly on geography: it was close enough to David-Horodok for visits and travel to shape local religious life. But it was also a center of the Karlin-Stolin Hasidic tradition. The YIVO Encyclopedia’s account of Pinsk places Karlin among the earliest Hasidic centers, associated with Aharon the Great and his successor Shelomoh. That regional history helps explain the standing of a Stolin prayer house in the town; it does not, by itself, establish how many local residents followed the dynasty.

The memorial book describes a second Hasidic lineage: the Ginzburg family of Horodok. Its account traces the line from Rabbi Wolf through Rabbi David and Rabbi Yosef to later descendants, including Reb Alterke and Reb Vova, and identifies Rabbi Israel Yosef as a central figure. A separate historical sketch in the same memorial book says that Rabbi Wolf—also called Rav Wolftsi—founded an independent Hasidic dynasty around the beginning of the nineteenth century. That sketch cautions that details of his life and exact date of death are unknown, and that his son Rabbi David seems to have had little influence. Rabbi Israel Yosef, by contrast, led a small following extending beyond town, to places including Lakhva, Turov, and Kożangródek.

This distinction matters: David-Horodok was not simply a satellite of Stolin. The local Horodoker dynasty had its own rebbes, family history, and followers, even as Stolin Hasidism had its own synagogue and external leadership. The memorial book records a [Stolin Hasidic synagogue](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_acf0b86bb0c4e62f357cbf9f) and a [Staliner shtibl](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_5244201c5dc571cba9ffa8aa); it is not clear from the supplied passages whether these refer to separate buildings or different names for the same congregation.

## Pilgrimage, leadership, and the route to Stolin

The memorial book remembers the roads as part of the religious world. On the eve of Rosh Hashanah, it says, Hasidim from Stolin, Turov, and Olbsk passed through David-Horodok on their way to Stolin. They brought the larger Hasidic world into town for a moment: travelers bound for a rebbe, moving through familiar streets during the season of prayer and gathering. This is the community’s remembered scene; the passage does not give a count or a precise date.

The traffic of religious authority also ran in other directions. Rabbi Israel Yosef traveled to Rabbi Motele of Chernobyl for the High Holy Days, carrying petitionary notes from his own Hasidim. The memorial book tells of a tense encounter in which a message from Stolin appears to have influenced how Rabbi Motele’s household received the Horodok rabbi. The story conveys both Rabbi Israel Yosef’s standing beyond his own town and the delicate relations among Hasidic courts. It is a remembered account, not independent confirmation of the episode.

In 1926, according to the book, Rabbi Israel Yehuda Kula came to David-Horodok through the influence of his Stolin rebbe, Rabbi Moshe Perlov. A shochet (ritual slaughterer) as well as a gifted musician, Kula led the Prayer for Dew at the Stolin Hasidim’s synagogue during Passover. The book recalls that worshippers from other synagogues—and Rabbi Dovidl, the elderly town rabbi—came to hear him. His story also exposes friction: a dispute among butchers and ritual slaughterers intensified around his appointment, and the conflict reached Pinsk and Vilna. The synagogue was thus a place not only of devotion and music, but of work, authority, and communal negotiation.

## Worship across factional lines

Hasidic and non-Hasidic identities did not keep all residents apart. The memorial book’s portrait of Rabbi Shapira, the town’s recognized rabbi, shows him joining the Stolin and Karlin Hasidim for Hallel on Passover nights and for Torah processions on Shemini Atzeret. In turn, the Hasidic community came to his home for Kiddush on Simchat Torah, and he visited rebbes from Karlin and Stolin when they came to town. These scenes do not erase disagreements between Hasidim and mitnagdim; they show how ritual hospitality and shared respect could cross those lines.

The book’s independent record on Stolin Hasidism is rich in names and recollections, but it is not a complete census of religious life. Its account names leaders and prayer houses while leaving many congregants’ family histories and individual destinations undocumented. That limitation is especially important when reading a memorial book written after catastrophe: its surviving testimony preserves a community’s memory, not every life that belonged to it.

## The rupture of war

The broader historical record establishes the setting in which this religious world was destroyed. Yad Vashem’s Encyclopedia of the Ghettos identifies Dawidgródek as the Polish name for the town before the war, with Davyd-Haradok and David-Gorodok among its other names. It estimates that about 3,000 Jews—roughly a third of the population—lived there between the world wars. After the German occupation, the town’s Jewish men were murdered in August 1941; women and children were driven out, and a ghetto was established in 1942. Yad Vashem records that the ghetto was liquidated on September 10, 1942.

This independent account supplies what a story centered on synagogue life cannot: the scale and sequence of the destruction. It does not document the Stolin synagogue’s congregants individually or independently verify the memorial book’s stories about rebbes, pilgrims, and prayer leaders. YIVO’s Pinsk entry adds the regional history of Karlin as an early Hasidic center, but neither it nor Yad Vashem is testimony to the local scenes remembered in the book. The surviving evidence therefore leaves important questions open: who among the named congregants survived, where families went after expulsion, and what happened to the buildings and objects of worship.
